generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, searching for evidence is rarely a quick lookup. Students here study sport, physical activity, performance and health, but they lean on different evidence. A sport scientist reads lab data, a coach weighs training observations, a manager checks participation figures. Across all of them, finding sources means exploring a question the field still debates, then searching again with better terms. That exploratory, iterative and planned approach is what academic searching asks of you.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two sport and exercise science students given the same essay question and told to find sources for it.

Tom types the whole essay question into a search box, glances at the first few results, and picks the one at the top. The search is over in a minute. Tom has treated this like looking up a fact: one attempt, no plan, and whatever came first. He had no sense of what a good physiology study would look like, or how to look again. This is everyday searching.

Amara starts by asking what the question is really about and what sort of study would answer it. She tries a few terms, sees what the literature returns, and searches again with better words when the first set is too broad. Her search into sleep and recovery takes longer, but it is exploratory, iterative and planned. This is academic searching.

Both students searched. Only Amara treated searching as a discipline rather than a quick lookup.
generatedProse.summary: Academic searching in the School of Sport is more than looking something up. It is exploratory, because you are following a question the field still debates; iterative, because you search again with better words; and strategy-driven, because you plan before you start. Whether you end up in sport science, coaching, management or therapy, you can now explain what academic searching is and tell it apart from the everyday searching you already do. The next lesson looks at what makes a search effective.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's approach academic rather than everyday?

items.text: She planned what she wanted, tried some terms, and searched again with better ones.
She finished the search more quickly than Tom did.
She typed the whole essay question into the search box.
She picked the result at the top of the list.

feedback.correct: That's right. Planning, trying terms and searching again is academic searching in action.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID differently, beyond finishing fast or taking the first result.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara was academic because she planned, tried terms and searched again. Finishing fast, typing the whole question or taking the top result are all the everyday approach.
